nodes.name: signed group-set
nodes.statement: A signed group-set is defined to be a pair $(G,\Phi)$ satisfying the following conditions: \begin{enumerate}\item[(1)] $G$ is a group \item[(2)] $\Phi$ is a set with a given left action $(g,x)\mapsto gx$ by the product group $G\times \{\pm 1\}$. This action defines a pair of commuting left actions, by $G$ and $\{\pm 1\}$ on $\Phi$. \item[(3)] There is a specified partition $\Phi=\Phi^{+}\cup \Phi^{-}$ of $\Phi$ in to two disjoint subsets which are interchanged by the action of $-1$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A group $G$ together with a $G\times\{\pm1\}$-set $\Phi$ split into positive and negative roots interchanged by $-1$.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I
differentia: $\Phi$ is a set with a given left action $(g,x)\mapsto gx$ by the product group $G\times \{\pm 1\}$
There is a specified partition $\Phi=\Phi^{+}\cup \Phi^{-}$ of $\Phi$ in to two disjoint subsets which are interchanged by the action of $-1$

nodes.name: root system and positive roots of $(G,\Phi)$
nodes.statement: We call $\Phi$ the root system of $(G,\Phi)$ and $\Phi^{+}$ the set of positive roots.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I

nodes.name: $\Phi_g$, the inversion set of $g$
nodes.statement: For every $g\in G$, we define the subset $ \Phi_{g}:=\Phi^{+}\cap g(\Phi^{-})$. This is the set of positive roots which are made negative by $g^{-1}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\Phi_g$ is the set of positive roots sent to negative roots by $g^{-1}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I
nodes.genus: set of positive roots which are made negative by $g^{-1}$

nodes.name: weak order of a signed group-set
nodes.statement: The weak order of $(G,\Phi)$ is defined to be the set $\mathcal{L}:=\{\, \Phi_{g}\mid g\in G\,\}$ of subsets of $\Phi^{+}$, partially ordered by inclusion.
nodes.statement_short: The poset $\mathcal{L}=\{\Phi_g\mid g\in G\}$ of inversion sets ordered by inclusion.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I
nodes.genus: set $\mathcal{L}:=\{\, \Phi_{g}\mid g\in G\,\}$ of subsets of $\Phi^{+}$

nodes.name: rootoidal signed group-set
nodes.statement: $(G,S)$ is said to be rootoidal if the following additional conditions hold: \begin{enumerate}\item[(4)] If $g\in {G}$ with $\Phi_{g}=\emptyset$ then $g=1_{G}$. \item[(5)] $\mathcal{L}$ is a complete meet semilattice i.e. each of its non-empty subsets has a meet (greatest lower boind). \item[(6)] Given a non-empty family $(A_{i})_{i\in I}$ of $\mathcal{L}$ and $B\in \mathcal{L}$ such that $A_{i}\cap B=\emptyset$ for all $i\in I$, if the join (least upper bound) $A:=\bigvee_{i\in I} A_{i}$ exists in $\mathcal{L}$, then $A\cap B=\emptyset$. (This condition is called the JTP). \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A signed group-set is rootoidal when trivial inversion set forces identity, $\mathcal{L}$ is a complete meet semilattice, and the JTP holds.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I
differentia: $\mathcal{L}$ is a complete meet semilattice i.e. each of its non-empty subsets has a meet (greatest lower boind)

Given a non-empty family $(A_{i})_{i\in I}$ of $\mathcal{L}$ and $B\in \mathcal{L}$ such that $A_{i}\cap B=\emptyset$ for all $i\in I$, if the join (least upper bound) $A:=\bigvee_{i\in I} A_{i}$ exists in $\mathcal{L}$, then $A\cap B=\emptyset$

nodes.name: complete signed group-set
nodes.statement: $(G,\Phi)$ is said to be complete if $\mathcal{L}$ has a maximum element, or equivalently if the weak order of $\mathcal{L}$ is a complete lattice.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I
differentia: the weak order of $\mathcal{L}$ is a complete lattice

nodes.name: Coxeter systems give signed group-sets whose weak order is the usual weak order
nodes.statement: For a Coxeter system $(W,S)$, the usual standard root system $\Phi$ of $(W,S)$ together with a choice $\Phi^{+}$ of positive roots give rise to a signed group-set $(W,\Phi)$. The weak-order of this signed group set is exactly the usual weak order of $W$.
nodes.statement_short: The standard root system of a Coxeter system yields a signed group-set recovering the classical weak order.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I
assumptions: For a Coxeter system $(W,S)$, the usual standard root system $\Phi$ of $(W,S)$ together with a choice $\Phi^{+}$ of positive roots give rise to a signed group-set $(W,\Phi)$.
conclusions: The weak-order of this signed group set is exactly the usual weak order of $W$.

nodes.name: Standing setup for the main theorem: $G=O(V)$ acting on the unit sphere
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a real Euclidean space and $G=O(V)$ be the orthogonal group of $V$. Let $\Phi$ be the unit sphere in $V$, with its natural action by $G\times\{\pm 1\}$. Fix a vector-space total ordering $\preceq$ of $V$ and let $\Phi^{+}:=\{\, v\in \Phi\mid v>0\,\}$ and $\Phi^{-}:=-\Phi^{+}$.
nodes.statement_short: Take $G=O(V)$, $\Phi$ the unit sphere of $V$, and $\Phi^{+}$ the vectors positive for a fixed vector-space total ordering.

nodes.name: Main Theorem: $(O(V),\Phi)$ is a complete rootoidal signed group-set
nodes.statement: The pair $(G,\Phi)$ defined above is a complete, rootoidal, signed group-set.
nodes.statement_short: $O(V)$ on the unit sphere is a complete rootoidal signed group-set.
assumptions: Let $V$ be a real Euclidean space and $G=O(V)$ be the orthogonal group of $V$.
Let $\Phi$ be the unit sphere in $V$, with its natural action by $G\times\{\pm 1\}$.
Fix a vector-space total ordering $\preceq$ of $V$ and let $\Phi^{+}:=\{\, v\in \Phi\mid v>0\,\}$ and $\Phi^{-}:=-\Phi^{+}$.
conclusions: The pair $(G,\Phi)$ defined above is a complete, rootoidal, signed group-set.

nodes.name: Sufficient conditions for a complete rootoidal signed group-set
nodes.statement: a signed group-set $(G,\Phi)$ with weak order $L$ is a complete rootoidal signed group-set if the following conditions hold: \begin{enumerate}\item[(7)] If $g\in {G}$ with $\Phi_{g}=\emptyset$ then $g=1_{a}$. \item[(8)] $L$ is a complete join semilattice i.e. each of subsets has a join \item[(9)] If $A\in \mathcal{L}$, then $\Phi^{+}\setminus A\in \mathcal{L}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Trivial-inversion-set, complete join semilattice, and closure of $\mathcal{L}$ under complement suffice for completeness and rootoidality.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyer, Groupoids, Root Systems and Weak Order I
assumptions: a signed group-set $(G,\Phi)$ with weak order $L$
conclusions: is a complete rootoidal signed group-set if the following conditions hold: \begin{enumerate}\item[(7)] If $g\in {G}$ with $\Phi_{g}=\emptyset$ then $g=1_{a}$. \item[(8)] $L$ is a complete join semilattice i.e. each of subsets has a join \item[(9)] If $A\in \mathcal{L}$, then $\Phi^{+}\setminus A\in \mathcal{L}$. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Proof that conditions (7)-(9) suffice
nodes.statement: Indeed, (8) and (9) imply that $L$ is a complete meet semi-lattice by duality. To prove that the JTP holds, let $A_{i}$, $B$ be as in its statement. By (9), $A_{i}\subseteq \Phi^{+}\setminus B\in \mathcal{L}$ for all $i$, so by definition of join, $A=\bigvee A_{i}\subseteq \Phi^{+}\setminus B$ and $A\cap B=\emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: Dualize (8)+(9) to get meet-completeness, then derive the JTP by placing every $A_i$ inside the complement of $B$.

nodes.name: Meet-completeness by duality
nodes.statement: Indeed, (8) and (9) imply that $L$ is a complete meet semi-lattice by duality.
nodes.statement_short: Conditions (8) and (9) give a complete meet semilattice by duality.

nodes.name: Verification of the JTP
nodes.statement: To prove that the JTP holds, let $A_{i}$, $B$ be as in its statement. By (9), $A_{i}\subseteq \Phi^{+}\setminus B\in \mathcal{L}$ for all $i$, so by definition of join, $A=\bigvee A_{i}\subseteq \Phi^{+}\setminus B$ and $A\cap B=\emptyset$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound every $A_i$ by $\Phi^{+}\setminus B$, so the join misses $B$.

nodes.name: Set-theoretic notation $\subseteq$, $\in$, $X\backslash Y$
nodes.statement: If $X$ and $Y$ are sets, we use $Y \subseteq X$ to denote that $Y$ is a subset of $X$ or equal to $X$. The notation $x \in X$ is used to denote that $x$ is an element of $X$. If $X$ and $Y$ are sets with $Y \subseteq X$, we use $X\backslash Y$ to denote the set $\{x \in X | x \not\in Y\}$.

nodes.name: partially ordered set (poset)
nodes.statement: A partially ordered set or poset is a set $P$ equipped with a binary relation $\leq$ such that for all $x, y, $ and $z \in P$, \begin{enumerate} \item $x \leq x$, \item $x \leq y$ and $y \leq x$ imply $x = y$, \item $x \leq y$ and $y \leq z$ imply $x \leq z$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.origin_citation: Davey & Priestley, Introduction to Lattices and Order
nodes.genus: set $P$ equipped with a binary relation $\leq$

nodes.name: totally ordered poset
nodes.statement: A poset $P$ with binary operation $\leq$ is totally ordered if given any pair of elements $\{x, y \} \in P$ we have either $x \leq y$ or $y \leq x$.
nodes.origin_citation: Davey & Priestley, Introduction to Lattices and Order
differentia: given any pair of elements $\{x, y \} \in P$ we have either $x \leq y$ or $y \leq x$

nodes.name: chain
nodes.statement: A poset $P$ is a {\bf chain} if for all $x, y \in P$, either $x \leq y$ or $y \leq x$.
nodes.origin_citation: Davey & Priestley, Introduction to Lattices and Order
differentia: for all $x, y \in P$, either $x \leq y$ or $y \leq x$

nodes.name: order isomorphic posets and order isomorphism
nodes.statement: Two posets $P$ and $Q$ are said to be {\bf order isomorphic} if there exists a map $\phi$ from $P$ onto $Q$ such that $x \leq y$ in $P$ if and only if $\phi(x) \leq \phi(y)$ in $Q$. Such a map $\phi$ is called an order isomorphism from $P$ to $Q$.
nodes.statement_short: Two posets are order isomorphic when some onto map preserves and reflects the order.
nodes.origin_citation: Davey & Priestley, Introduction to Lattices and Order
differentia: there exists a map $\phi$ from $P$ onto $Q$ such that $x \leq y$ in $P$ if and only if $\phi(x) \leq \phi(y)$ in $Q$

nodes.name: dual poset $P^{\delta}$
nodes.statement: Given a partially ordered set $P$ with order relation $\leq_{P}$, its dual, $P^{\delta}$, is the poset which is equal to $P$ as a set, with binary relation $\leq_{P^{\delta}}$ given by $x \leq_{P^{\delta}} y$ if and only if $y \leq_{P} x$.
nodes.origin_citation: Davey & Priestley, Introduction to Lattices and Order
nodes.genus: poset which is equal to $P$ as a set
differentia: $x \leq_{P^{\delta}} y$ if and only if $y \leq_{P} x$

nodes.name: upper bound
nodes.statement: an element $x \in P$ is an {\bf upper bound} for $S$ if $y \leq x$ for all $y \in S$.
nodes.origin_citation: Davey & Priestley, Introduction to Lattices and Order

nodes.name: least upper bound $\bigvee S$ and join $x \vee y$
nodes.statement: An element $l \in P$ is a {\bf least upper bound} for $S$ if $l$ is an upper bound for $S$ and if $x$ is another upper bound for $S$, then $l \leq x$. The least upper bound of the set $S$ is denoted by $\bigvee S$ when it exists or $\bigvee_P S$ if it is unclear which poset we are considering. In the case of two elements, we let $x \vee y$ denote the least upper bound of the two element set $\{x, y\}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\bigvee S$ is the smallest upper bound of $S$; $x \vee y$ denotes the binary case.
nodes.origin_citation: Davey & Priestley, Introduction to Lattices and Order
differentia: if $x$ is another upper bound for $S$, then $l \leq x$

nodes.name: lower bounds and greatest lower bounds $\bigwedge S$
nodes.statement: {\bf Lower bounds } and {\bf greatest lower bounds} are defined dually with $\bigwedge S$ denoting the greatest lower bound of the set $S$ and $x \wedge y$ denoting the greatest lower bound of the set $\{x, y\}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Davey & Priestley, Introduction to Lattices and Order

nodes.name: Lattice and complete lattice
nodes.statement: Let $P$ be a non-empty poset. If $x\wedge y$ and $x \vee y$ exist in $P$ for all $x, y \in P$, we say $P$ is a {\bf Lattice}. If $\bigwedge S$ and $\bigvee S$ exist in $P$ for every subset $S$ of $P$, then we say $P$ is a {\bf complete lattice}.
nodes.statement_short: A lattice has all binary meets and joins; a complete lattice has them for every subset.
nodes.origin_citation: Davey & Priestley, Introduction to Lattices and Order
differentia: $x\wedge y$ and $x \vee y$ exist in $P$ for all $x, y \in P$
If $\bigwedge S$ and $\bigvee S$ exist in $P$ for every subset $S$ of $P$, then we say $P$ is a {\bf complete lattice}

nodes.name: directed subset
nodes.statement: If $S$ is a non-empty subset of a poset $P$, $S$ is said to be {\bf directed} if for every pair of elements $x, y \in S$, there exists $z \in S$, such that $z$ is an upper bound for the set $\{x, y\}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Davey & Priestley, Introduction to Lattices and Order
differentia: for every pair of elements $x, y \in S$, there exists $z \in S$, such that $z$ is an upper bound for the set $\{x, y\}$

nodes.name: The unit sphere $S^n$ and the positive/negative roots $\Phi_n^+, \Phi_n^-$
nodes.statement: We let $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ denote The Euclidean $(n + 1)$ space, with standard basis $\{e_1, e_2, \dots , e_{n + 1}\}$. The standard inner product or dot product on $\Bbb{R}^{n+1}$ is denoted by $< , >$. The unit sphere in $\Bbb{R}^{n+1}$ is $$S^n = \{(x_1, x_2, \dots , x_{n+1}) \in \Bbb{R}^{n+1} | x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \dots + x_{n+1}^2 = 1\}$$ and $\Phi_n^+$ is used to denote the set $$\Phi_n^+ = \{(x_1, x_2, \dots , x_{n + 1}) \in S^n | x_m = <x, e_m> > 0 \ \ \mbox{where} \ \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | x_i \not= 0\} \}.$$ For its negative $ -\Phi_n^+ $, we use $$\Phi_n^- = \{(x_1, x_2, \dots , x_{n + 1}) \in S^n | x_m = <x, e_m> < 0 \ \ \mbox{where} \ \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | x_i \not= 0\} \}.$$ Note that $S^n = \Phi_n^+ \cup \Phi_n^-$ and $\Phi_n^+ \cap \Phi_n^-$ is empty.
nodes.statement_short: $\Phi_n^{\pm}$ are the points of $S^n$ whose last nonzero coordinate is positive (resp. negative); they partition $S^n$.
differentia: $$\Phi_n^+ = \{(x_1, x_2, \dots , x_{n + 1}) \in S^n | x_m = <x, e_m> > 0 \ \ \mbox{where} \ \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | x_i \not= 0\} \}.$$
$$\Phi_n^- = \{(x_1, x_2, \dots , x_{n + 1}) \in S^n | x_m = <x, e_m> < 0 \ \ \mbox{where} \ \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | x_i \not= 0\} \}.$$

nodes.name: Orthogonal group notation and orthogonal direct sums $V_1 \bot V_2$
nodes.statement: For a Euclidean space $V$, we let $O(V)$ denote the orthogonal group of $V$. Sometimes we use $O_{k}$ to denote the orthogonal transformations of $\Bbb{R}^{k}$. For any $T \in O_{n + 1}$, we have $<T(x), T(y)> = <x, y>$ for all $x, y \in \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$. We write $x\bot y$ to denote that $<x, y> = 0$ for $x, y \in \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$. If $V_1$ and $V_2$ are subspaces of $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $V_1 + V_2 = V$ and $<v_1, v_2> = 0$ for all $v_1 \in V_1$ and $v_2 \in V_2$, then we say that $V_2$ is the orthogonal complement of $V_1$ in $V$ and we write the sum as $V = V_1 \bot V_2$. If $T_1 \in O(V_1)$ and $T_2 \in O(V_2)$ and $V = V_1 \bot V_2$, the linear transformation $T = T_1 \bot T_2$ is the unique linear transformation in $O(V)$ with the property that $T(v_1) = T_1(v_1)$ and $T(v_2) = T_2(v_2)$ for all $v_1 \in V_1$ and $v_2 \in V_2$. We let $I_V$ denote the identity transformation on $V$ and we let $1_{e_i}$ denote the identity transformation on the subspace $\Bbb{R}e_i$ of $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Notation for $O(V)$, $O_k$, orthogonality $x\bot y$, orthogonal complements $V=V_1\bot V_2$, and split maps $T=T_1\bot T_2$.

nodes.name: Imbedding of $\Bbb{R}^k$, the norm $||x||$ and closure $\bar{X}$
nodes.statement: We have a natural imbedding of $\Bbb{R}^{k}, k < n$ in $R^{n + 1}$ where we identify $\Bbb{R}^{k}$ with the set $\{(x_1, x_2, \dots , x_{n + 1} )| x_m = 0 \ \mbox{if} \ m > k \}$. This induces an imbedding of $S^{k - 1}, \Phi_{k - 1}^+$ and $\Phi_{k - 1}^-$ in $R^{n + 1}$. For $x = (x_1, x_2, \dots , x_{n + 1}) \in \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$, we let $||x|| = \sqrt{x_1^2 + x_2^2 + \dots + x_{n + 1}^2}$. The topological closure of a set $X \subseteq \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with respect to the metric defined by this norm on $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ is denoted by $\bar{X}$.
nodes.statement_short: Identify $\Bbb{R}^k$ with the vectors whose coordinates vanish above index $k$; $||\cdot||$ is the Euclidean norm and $\bar{X}$ the closure.

nodes.name: cone, convex cone and pointed convex cone
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product $<- , ->$. A subset $C \subseteq V$ is called a {\bf cone} if $C$ satisfies conditions (1) and (2) below: \begin{enumerate} \item $0 \in C$, \item If $v \in C$, then $\Bbb{R}_{\geq 0}v \subseteq C$. \noindent \leftline{C is called a {\bf convex cone} if it also satisfies the property:} \item If $u, v \in C$, then $u + v \in C$. \noindent A convex cone $C$ is a {\bf pointed convex cone} if it is a convex cone and satisfies the property: \item $C \cap (-C) = \{0\}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: A cone contains $0$ and all non-negative rescalings; convex adds closure under sums; pointed adds $C\cap(-C)=\{0\}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Fenchel, Convex cones, sets, and functions
differentia: If $u, v \in C$, then $u + v \in C$

nodes.name: Rays in a cone correspond bijectively to its points on the unit sphere
nodes.statement: Note that for any cone $C$ contained in $R^k$, $k > 0$, if $x \not= 0 \in C$, the {\bf ray} $(x) = \{rx | r \in \Bbb{R}_{\geq 0}\}$ is contained in $C$. This ray intersects the unit sphere $S^{k - 1}$ at exactly one point $\frac{x}{||x||}$. Thus we have a one to one correspondence between the rays in $C$ and the points on the unit sphere $S^{k - 1}$ which are in $C$.
nodes.statement_short: Each ray of a cone meets $S^{k-1}$ exactly once, giving a bijection rays $\leftrightarrow$ sphere points in $C$.

nodes.name: the cone $\widehat{X}$ generated by a subset of the sphere
nodes.statement: Let $X \subseteq S^n$, we use $\widehat{X}$ to denote the following cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$: $$\widehat{X} = \{rx | x \in X \ \mbox{and} \ r \in \Bbb{R}_{\geq 0} \} \ \mbox{if} \ X \not= \emptyset$$ and $\widehat{\emptyset} = \{0\}$.

nodes.name: Cone-sphere correspondence for $\widehat{X}$
nodes.statement: Let $X$ and $Y$ be subsets of $S^n$. \begin{enumerate} \item $X = \widehat{X} \cap S^n$ and if $C$ is any cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $X = C\cap S^n$, then $\widehat{X} = C$, \item $X\cap Y = \emptyset$, if and only if $\widehat{X} \cap \widehat{Y} = \{0\}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: $\widehat{X}$ is the unique cone meeting $S^n$ in $X$, and disjointness of $X,Y$ is equivalent to $\widehat{X}\cap\widehat{Y}=\{0\}$.
assumptions: Let $X$ and $Y$ be subsets of $S^n$.
conclusions: $X = \widehat{X} \cap S^n$ and if $C$ is any cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $X = C\cap S^n$, then $\widehat{X} = C$,
$X\cap Y = \emptyset$, if and only if $\widehat{X} \cap \widehat{Y} = \{0\}$.

nodes.name: Proof of the cone-sphere correspondence
nodes.statement:
Assertion (1) is trivial if $X = \emptyset$, so let us assume for now that $X 
ot= \emptyset$. We have $\widehat{X}$ is a union of rays, $\widehat{X} =  igcup_{x \in X, x 
ot= 0} (x)$. Since each ray $(x)$ where $x \in X$ cuts the unit sphere exactly once at $x$, we have $X = \widehat{X} \cap S^n$. If C is a cone with $C \cap S^n = X$, then $\widehat{X} \subseteq C$, since the entire ray $(x)$ is in $C$ if $x \in X$. On the other hand, if $c \in C$, the ray $(c)$ cuts the sphere $S^n$ at $ rac{c}{||c||} \in X$. Therefore $( rac{c}{||c||}) = (c) \in \widehat{X}$ and since $C$ is the union of such rays, we have $C \subseteq \widehat{X}$. This proves (1). We can now relax the assumption that $X 
ot= \emptyset$. It is easily seen that $\widehat{X} \cap \widehat{Y} = \widehat{X \cap Y}$. Assertion (2) follows from the observation that if $C$ is a cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$, then $C \cap S^n = \emptyset$ if and only if $C = \{0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $\widehat{X}$ as a union of rays and compare with an arbitrary cone $C$; then reduce (2) to $C\cap S^n=\emptyset \iff C=\{0\}$.

nodes.name: Assertion (1): $\widehat{X}$ is the unique cone cutting $S^n$ in $X$
nodes.statement: Assertion (1) is trivial if $X = \emptyset$, so let us assume for now that $X \not= \emptyset$. We have $\widehat{X}$ is a union of rays, $\widehat{X} = \bigcup_{x \in X, x \not= 0} (x)$. Since each ray $(x)$ where $x \in X$ cuts the unit sphere exactly once at $x$, we have $X = \widehat{X} \cap S^n$. If C is a cone with $C \cap S^n = X$, then $\widehat{X} \subseteq C$, since the entire ray $(x)$ is in $C$ if $x \in X$. On the other hand, if $c \in C$, the ray $(c)$ cuts the sphere $S^n$ at $\frac{c}{||c||} \in X$. Therefore $(\frac{c}{||c||}) = (c) \in \widehat{X}$ and since $C$ is the union of such rays, we have $C \subseteq \widehat{X}$. This proves (1).
nodes.statement_short: Decompose $\widehat{X}$ into rays, each meeting $S^n$ once, and sandwich an arbitrary cone $C$ between the two inclusions.

nodes.name: Assertion (2): disjointness criterion
nodes.statement: We can now relax the assumption that $X \not= \emptyset$. It is easily seen that $\widehat{X} \cap \widehat{Y} = \widehat{X \cap Y}$. Assertion (2) follows from the observation that if $C$ is a cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$, then $C \cap S^n = \emptyset$ if and only if $C = \{0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Use $\widehat{X}\cap\widehat{Y}=\widehat{X\cap Y}$ and the fact that a cone misses $S^n$ only when it is $\{0\}$.

nodes.name: Closure commutes with intersecting a convex cone with the sphere
nodes.statement: Let $A$ be a convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$, then $\overline{A \cap S^{n} } = \bar{A} \cap S^n$.
nodes.statement_short: For a convex cone $A$, $\overline{A\cap S^n} = \bar{A}\cap S^n$.
assumptions: Let $A$ be a convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$,
conclusions: $\overline{A \cap S^{n} } = \bar{A} \cap S^n$.

nodes.name: Proof that $\overline{A \cap S^n} = \bar{A} \cap S^n$
nodes.statement: Let $A \subset \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ be a convex cone. Since $ \bar{A} \cap S^n$ is closed and contains $A \cap S^{n}$, we have $\overline{A \cap S^{n} } \subseteq \bar{A} \cap S^n$. On the other hand, if $x \in \bar{A} \cap S^n$, then $||x|| = 1$ and we have a sequence of points $\{x_i\}_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ in $A$ such that $\lim_{i \to \infty}x_i = x$. Since $A$ is convex we have the sequence of points $\{\frac{x_i}{||x_i||}\}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \in \bar{A} \cap S^n$. Given any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $m$ such that $| ||x_i|| - 1 | = | ||x_i|| - ||x|| | \leq ||x_i - x|| < \epsilon $ for all $i \geq m$. Since $$||x - \frac{x_i}{||x_i||}|| \leq ||x - x_i|| + ||x_i - \frac{x_i}{||x_i||}|| = ||x - x_i|| + \frac{||x_i||(| \ ||x_i|| - 1|)}{||x_i||} \leq 2\epsilon$$ for $i \geq m$, we have that the sequence $\{\frac{x_i}{||x_i||}\}_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ converges to $x$ and $x \in \overline{A \cap S^{n} }$.
nodes.statement_short: One inclusion is closedness; for the reverse, normalize an approximating sequence and estimate $||x - x_i/||x_i|| ||$.

nodes.name: Easy inclusion from closedness
nodes.statement: Let $A \subset \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ be a convex cone. Since $ \bar{A} \cap S^n$ is closed and contains $A \cap S^{n}$, we have $\overline{A \cap S^{n} } \subseteq \bar{A} \cap S^n$.
nodes.statement_short: $\bar{A}\cap S^n$ is a closed set containing $A\cap S^n$.

nodes.name: Reverse inclusion by normalizing an approximating sequence
nodes.statement: On the other hand, if $x \in \bar{A} \cap S^n$, then $||x|| = 1$ and we have a sequence of points $\{x_i\}_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ in $A$ such that $\lim_{i \to \infty}x_i = x$. Since $A$ is convex we have the sequence of points $\{\frac{x_i}{||x_i||}\}_{i = 1}^{\infty} \in \bar{A} \cap S^n$. Given any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists $m$ such that $| ||x_i|| - 1 | = | ||x_i|| - ||x|| | \leq ||x_i - x|| < \epsilon $ for all $i \geq m$. Since $$||x - \frac{x_i}{||x_i||}|| \leq ||x - x_i|| + ||x_i - \frac{x_i}{||x_i||}|| = ||x - x_i|| + \frac{||x_i||(| \ ||x_i|| - 1|)}{||x_i||} \leq 2\epsilon$$ for $i \geq m$, we have that the sequence $\{\frac{x_i}{||x_i||}\}_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ converges to $x$ and $x \in \overline{A \cap S^{n} }$.
nodes.statement_short: Normalize $x_i \to x$ and bound $||x - x_i/||x_i||||$ by $2\epsilon$.

nodes.name: closed half space $H_u$, hyperplane $H(u)$ and open half space $H_u^{int}$
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product $<- , ->$. For any fixed $u \in V$, we let $H_u$ denote {\bf the closed half space} $H_u = \{v \in V | <v, u> \leq 0 \}$. We let $H(u)$ denote the {\bf hyperplane} $\{ v \in V | <v, u> = 0 \}$ and we let $H_u^{int}$ denote the {\bf open half space } $\{ v \in V | <v, u> < 0 \}$. \\ We will use the notation $H^V_u, H^V(u)$, and $H^{Vint}_u$ when we want to emphasize the underlying vector space.\\
nodes.statement_short: $H_u$, $H(u)$, $H_u^{int}$ are the sets where $<v,u>$ is $\leq 0$, $=0$, $<0$ respectively.

$H_u^{int}$ denote the {\bf open half space } $\{ v \in V | <v, u> < 0 \}$

nodes.name: Rigidity of half-space containment
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product \\$<- , ->$. If $u, v \in V$ with $H(u) \subseteq H_v$, then $H(u) = H(v)$. Consequently if $u, v \in V$ with $H_u \subseteq H_v$, then $H_u = H_v$. Also $v_1 = \frac{-v}{||v||} \in H_v$ is the unique vector of norm one in $H_v$ with the property that $H_{v} = H_{-v_1}$.
nodes.statement_short: A hyperplane inside a half space forces equality of hyperplanes and of half spaces, and pins down the unit normal.
assumptions: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product \\$<- , ->$.
If $u, v \in V$ with $H(u) \subseteq H_v$,

Consequently if $u, v \in V$ with $H_u \subseteq H_v$, then $H_u = H_v$.
Also $v_1 = \frac{-v}{||v||} \in H_v$ is the unique vector of norm one in $H_v$ with the property that $H_{v} = H_{-v_1}$.

nodes.name: Proof of the half-space rigidity lemma
nodes.statement: Suppose $u, v \in V$ with $H(u) \subseteq H_v = \{x \in V | <x, v> \leq 0 \}$. If $x \in H(u)$ with the property that $<x, v> \not= 0$, then $\{x,-x\} \in H(u)$ and either $<x, v> > 0$ or $<-x, v> > 0$ giving a contradiction. Hence $H(u) \subseteq H(v)$ and we have equality by comparing dimensions. If $H_u \subseteq H_v$, then $H(u) \subseteq H_v$ and therefore $H(u) = H(v)$. Now $V = <v> \bot H(v) = <u> \bot H(u) = <u> \bot H(v)$ and $u = cv$. Since $H_u \subseteq H_v$, $-u \in H_v$, hence $<-u, v> = <-cv, v> < 0$ and we have $c > 0$. Therefore $H_u = H_v$. Let $v_1 \in H_v$ such that $H_{-v_1} = H_{v}$, then as above, $-v_1 = cv$ for some $c > 0$. If we assume $||v_1|| = 1$, then we must have $v_1 = \frac{-v}{||v||} $.
nodes.statement_short: Antipodal pairs in $H(u)$ force $H(u)\subseteq H(v)$; compare dimensions, then fix the sign of the scalar $c$.

nodes.name: $H(u) \subseteq H_v$ implies $H(u) = H(v)$
nodes.statement: Suppose $u, v \in V$ with $H(u) \subseteq H_v = \{x \in V | <x, v> \leq 0 \}$. If $x \in H(u)$ with the property that $<x, v> \not= 0$, then $\{x,-x\} \in H(u)$ and either $<x, v> > 0$ or $<-x, v> > 0$ giving a contradiction. Hence $H(u) \subseteq H(v)$ and we have equality by comparing dimensions.
nodes.statement_short: If some $x\in H(u)$ had $<x,v>\ne0$ then $x$ or $-x$ leaves $H_v$; then compare dimensions.

nodes.name: $H_u \subseteq H_v$ implies $H_u = H_v$
nodes.statement: If $H_u \subseteq H_v$, then $H(u) \subseteq H_v$ and therefore $H(u) = H(v)$. Now $V = <v> \bot H(v) = <u> \bot H(u) = <u> \bot H(v)$ and $u = cv$. Since $H_u \subseteq H_v$, $-u \in H_v$, hence $<-u, v> = <-cv, v> < 0$ and we have $c > 0$. Therefore $H_u = H_v$.
nodes.statement_short: Write $u = cv$ from the hyperplane equality and use $-u \in H_v$ to force $c > 0$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the unit normal $v_1$
nodes.statement: Let $v_1 \in H_v$ such that $H_{-v_1} = H_{v}$, then as above, $-v_1 = cv$ for some $c > 0$. If we assume $||v_1|| = 1$, then we must have $v_1 = \frac{-v}{||v||} $.
nodes.statement_short: Normalizing $-v_1 = cv$ with $c>0$ leaves only $v_1 = -v/||v||$.

nodes.name: Non-emptiness of the intersection of two open half spaces
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product \\$<- , ->$ and let $u, v \in V$. Then $H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int}$ is non-empty if $ u \not= -cv, \ c > 0$.
nodes.statement_short: Two open half spaces meet unless their normals are negative multiples of each other.
assumptions: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product \\$<- , ->$ and let $u, v \in V$.
conclusions: Then $H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int}$ is non-empty if $ u \not= -cv, \ c > 0$.

nodes.name: Proof that two open half spaces intersect
nodes.statement: Let $u, v \in V$. Clearly $H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int} = \emptyset$ if $u = -cv$ for some $c > 0$ in $\Bbb{R}$. Lets assume that $u \not= -cv, c > 0$. Suppose that $H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int} = \emptyset$, then if $x \in H_u^{int}$ we must have $x \not\in H_v^{int}$ and $<x, v> \geq 0$ and $H_u^{int} \subseteq H_{-v}$. Taking closures, we get $H_u \subseteq H_{-v}$ and by Lemma \ref{hyper} $H_u = H_{-v}$ and $u = -cv$ for some $c > 0$ giving us a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Assume the intersection is empty, take closures to get $H_u = H_{-v}$ by the rigidity lemma, and contradict $u \ne -cv$.

nodes.name: The degenerate direction
nodes.statement: Let $u, v \in V$. Clearly $H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int} = \emptyset$ if $u = -cv$ for some $c > 0$ in $\Bbb{R}$.
nodes.statement_short: If $u = -cv$ the two open half spaces are visibly disjoint.

nodes.name: Contradiction in the non-degenerate case
nodes.statement: Lets assume that $u \not= -cv, c > 0$. Suppose that $H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int} = \emptyset$, then if $x \in H_u^{int}$ we must have $x \not\in H_v^{int}$ and $<x, v> \geq 0$ and $H_u^{int} \subseteq H_{-v}$. Taking closures, we get $H_u \subseteq H_{-v}$ and by Lemma \ref{hyper} $H_u = H_{-v}$ and $u = -cv$ for some $c > 0$ giving us a contradiction.
nodes.statement_short: Emptiness would force $H_u^{int}\subseteq H_{-v}$, hence $H_u = H_{-v}$ and $u = -cv$.

nodes.name: Closure of the intersection of two open half spaces
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product \\$<- , ->$ and let $u, v \in V$ for which $ u \not= -cv, \ c > 0$. Then $$\overline{H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int}} = H_u \cap H_v.$$
nodes.statement_short: $\overline{H_u^{int}\cap H_v^{int}} = H_u \cap H_v$ whenever $u \ne -cv$ for $c>0$.
assumptions: Let $V$ be a Euclidean space with positive definite inner product \\$<- , ->$ and let $u, v \in V$ for which $ u \not= -cv, \ c > 0$.
conclusions: Then $$\overline{H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int}} = H_u \cap H_v.$$

nodes.name: Proof of the closure formula for $H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int}$
nodes.statement:
Let $u$ and $v$ be as in the statement of the lemma and let $C = H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int}$. Clearly the lemma is true if $u = cv$ for some $c > 0$. Therefore we will assume that $u 
ot= cv$ for any $c \in \Bbb{R}$ for the rest of the proof. In this case $H(u) 
ot= H(v)$. Since $\overline{H_u^{int}} = H_u$ and $\overline{H_v^{int}} = H_v$, we have $C \subseteq H_{u} \cap H_{v}$ and since $H_{u} \cap H_{v}$ is a closed set, we have $ ar{C} \subseteq H_{u} \cap H_{v}$. To verify the opposite inclusion, consider $x \in H_{u} \cap H_v$. If $x \in C$, then $x \in  ar{C}$. Therefore we need only consider points $x$ where $<x, u> = 0$ or $<x, v> = 0$ or both. If $<x, u> = 0$ and $<x, v> > 0$, we have a sequence $\{x_i\}_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ in $H_{u}^{int}$ with $\lim_{i 	o \infty} x_i = x$. Now since $x \in H_{v}^{int}$ which is an open set, there exists an $m$ for which $x_i \in H_{v}^{int}$ for all $i \geq m$. Therefore $x_i \in C$ for all $i \geq m$ and $x \in  ar{C}$. A similar argument shows that if $<x, v> = 0$ and $<x, u> < 0$, we have $x \in  ar{C}$. Now if $<x, v> = 0$ and $<x, u> = 0$, then $x \in [H(u) \cap H(v)]$ which is a subspace of $H(v)$ of dimension $n - 2$ since $H(u) 
ot= H(v)$. Let $H = [H(u) \cap H(v)]$. It remains to show that $H \subseteq  ar{C}$. We consider $H$ as a hyperplane in $H(v)$. It is not difficult to see that if $y \in H(v)$, $<y, u> = < y, \pi(u)>$ where $\pi(u)$ is the orthogonal projection of $u$ onto the hyperplane $H(v)$. Therefore $$H = \{y \in H(v) | <y, \pi(u)> = 0 \} = H^{H(v)}(\pi(u))$$ as a hyperplane in $H(v)$. Now looking at the corresponding open half space in $H(v)$, we have $H_{\pi(u)}^{H(v){int}} = \{x \in H(v)| <x,\pi(u)> < 0\}$. By our reasoning above we know this is a subset of $ ar{C}$. Taking the closure within $H(v)$, we have $H^{H(v)}_{\pi(u)} = \overline{H_{\pi(u)}^{H(v)int} }\subseteq  ar{C}$ and $H = H^{H(v)}(\pi(u)) \subseteq  ar{C}$. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Prove both inclusions, handling boundary points by approximating sequences and treating $H(u)\cap H(v)$ inside $H(v)$ via the projection $\pi(u)$.

nodes.name: Set-up and reduction to $H(u) \ne H(v)$
nodes.statement: Let $u$ and $v$ be as in the statement of the lemma and let $C = H_u^{int} \cap H_v^{int}$. Clearly the lemma is true if $u = cv$ for some $c > 0$. Therefore we will assume that $u \not= cv$ for any $c \in \Bbb{R}$ for the rest of the proof. In this case $H(u) \not= H(v)$.
nodes.statement_short: Name $C = H_u^{int}\cap H_v^{int}$ and dispose of the case $u = cv$.

nodes.name: The inclusion $\bar{C} \subseteq H_u \cap H_v$
nodes.statement: Since $\overline{H_u^{int}} = H_u$ and $\overline{H_v^{int}} = H_v$, we have $C \subseteq H_{u} \cap H_{v}$ and since $H_{u} \cap H_{v}$ is a closed set, we have $\bar{C} \subseteq H_{u} \cap H_{v}$.
nodes.statement_short: $H_u\cap H_v$ is closed and contains $C$.

nodes.statement: To verify the opposite inclusion, consider $x \in H_{u} \cap H_v$. If $x \in C$, then $x \in \bar{C}$. Therefore we need only consider points $x$ where $<x, u> = 0$ or $<x, v> = 0$ or both. If $<x, u> = 0$ and $<x, v> > 0$, we have a sequence $\{x_i\}_{i = 1}^{\infty}$ in $H_{u}^{int}$ with $\lim_{i \to \infty} x_i = x$. Now since $x \in H_{v}^{int}$ which is an open set, there exists an $m$ for which $x_i \in H_{v}^{int}$ for all $i \geq m$. Therefore $x_i \in C$ for all $i \geq m$ and $x \in \bar{C}$. A similar argument shows that if $<x, v> = 0$ and $<x, u> < 0$, we have $x \in \bar{C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate such $x$ from inside the open half space, using openness of the other one.

nodes.name: Points on $H(u) \cap H(v)$ via the projection $\pi(u)$
nodes.statement: Now if $<x, v> = 0$ and $<x, u> = 0$, then $x \in [H(u) \cap H(v)]$ which is a subspace of $H(v)$ of dimension $n - 2$ since $H(u) \not= H(v)$. Let $H = [H(u) \cap H(v)]$. It remains to show that $H \subseteq \bar{C}$. We consider $H$ as a hyperplane in $H(v)$. It is not difficult to see that if $y \in H(v)$, $<y, u> = < y, \pi(u)>$ where $\pi(u)$ is the orthogonal projection of $u$ onto the hyperplane $H(v)$. Therefore $$H = \{y \in H(v) | <y, \pi(u)> = 0 \} = H^{H(v)}(\pi(u))$$ as a hyperplane in $H(v)$. Now looking at the corresponding open half space in $H(v)$, we have $H_{\pi(u)}^{H(v){int}} = \{x \in H(v)| <x,\pi(u)> < 0\}$. By our reasoning above we know this is a subset of $\bar{C}$. Taking the closure within $H(v)$, we have $H^{H(v)}_{\pi(u)} = \overline{H_{\pi(u)}^{H(v)int} }\subseteq \bar{C}$ and $H = H^{H(v)}(\pi(u)) \subseteq \bar{C}$. This completes the proof.
nodes.statement_short: Regard $H(u)\cap H(v)$ as the hyperplane $H^{H(v)}(\pi(u))$ inside $H(v)$ and reuse the previous case.

nodes.name: maximal pointed convex cone
nodes.statement: A pointed convex cone $D$ in a Euclidean space $V$ is called {\bf maximal} if $D \cap (-D) = \{0\}$ and $D \cup (-D) = V$.
nodes.genus: pointed convex cone $D$ in a Euclidean space $V$

nodes.name: A maximal pointed convex cone induces a total ordering of $V$
nodes.statement: Note that a maximal pointed convex cone in a Euclidean space $V$ defines a total ordering on $V$ given by $y \leq x$ if and only if $y - x \in D$. Also $D = \{v \in V | v \leq 0\}$.
nodes.statement_short: Setting $y \le x$ iff $y - x \in D$ makes $V$ totally ordered with $D$ the non-positive part.

nodes.name: support for a cone
nodes.statement: A closed half space $H_u$ is called a {\bf support for a cone} $C$ if $C \subseteq H_u$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the support of a maximal pointed convex cone
nodes.statement: Let $D$ be a maximal pointed convex cone in a Euclidean space $V$ with positive definite inner product $<-, - >$. Then $D$ has a unique support $H_v$, in $V$ and $H_v = \bar{D}$. Furthermore $H_v^{int} = \{x \in V | <x, v> < 0 \} \subset D$.
nodes.statement_short: A maximal pointed convex cone has exactly one supporting half space, which equals its closure and whose interior lies inside the cone.
assumptions: Let $D$ be a maximal pointed convex cone in a Euclidean space $V$ with positive definite inner product $<-, - >$.
conclusions: Then $D$ has a unique support $H_v$, in $V$ and $H_v = \bar{D}$.
Furthermore $H_v^{int} = \{x \in V | <x, v> < 0 \} \subset D$.

nodes.name: Proof of uniqueness of the support
nodes.statement: According to Corollary 1 to Theorem 1 of Fenchel \cite{Fenchel}, a maximal pointed convex cone $D$ in $V$, has a support $H_{v}$, where $D \subseteq H_{v}$. Now since $D \cup (-D) = V$ we have $H_v^{int} = \{x \in V | <x, v> < 0 \} \subseteq D$. Otherwise we would have $x \in (-D)$ with $<x, v> < 0$ and thus $<-x, v> > 0$ for $-x \in D$ giving us a contradiction. Thus we have $\overline{H_v^{int}} = H_{v} \subseteq \bar{D}$. On the other hand $\bar{D} \subseteq H_{v}$ since $D \subseteq H_{v}$, therefore $\bar{D} = H_v$. Suppose that $H_{u}$ is also a support. Then as above, we have $\bar{D} = H_u$ and hence $H_u = H_v$.
nodes.statement_short: Import Fenchel's existence of a support, show $H_v^{int}\subseteq D$ by an antipodal contradiction, then squeeze $\bar{D} = H_v$.

nodes.name: Existence of a support and identification with $\bar{D}$
nodes.statement: According to Corollary 1 to Theorem 1 of Fenchel \cite{Fenchel}, a maximal pointed convex cone $D$ in $V$, has a support $H_{v}$, where $D \subseteq H_{v}$. Now since $D \cup (-D) = V$ we have $H_v^{int} = \{x \in V | <x, v> < 0 \} \subseteq D$. Otherwise we would have $x \in (-D)$ with $<x, v> < 0$ and thus $<-x, v> > 0$ for $-x \in D$ giving us a contradiction. Thus we have $\overline{H_v^{int}} = H_{v} \subseteq \bar{D}$. On the other hand $\bar{D} \subseteq H_{v}$ since $D \subseteq H_{v}$, therefore $\bar{D} = H_v$.
nodes.statement_short: Cite Fenchel for a support $H_v$, get $H_v^{int}\subseteq D$ by antipodal contradiction, then $\bar{D}=H_v$.

nodes.name: Uniqueness of the support
nodes.statement: Suppose that $H_{u}$ is also a support. Then as above, we have $\bar{D} = H_u$ and hence $H_u = H_v$.
nodes.statement_short: Any other support also equals $\bar{D}$, hence coincides with $H_v$.

nodes.name: Classification of maximal pointed convex cones by ordered orthonormal bases
nodes.statement: Let $V$ be a finite dimensional Euclidean space of dimension $n$ with positive definite inner product $< - , - >$. The following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item D is a maximal pointed convex cone in V, \item There exists an ordered basis $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ of $V$ with $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_i \in \Bbb{R}, c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\},$$ \item There exists an ordered orthonormal basis $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ of $V$ with $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_i \in \Bbb{R}, c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}.$$ \end{enumerate} Moreover the map taking $D$ to $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ is a bijection from the maximal pointed convex cones in $V$ to the set of ordered orthonormal bases of $V$. The orthogonal group $O(V)$ acts simply transitively on the set of maximal pointed convex cones in $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Maximal pointed convex cones correspond bijectively to ordered orthonormal bases, and $O(V)$ acts simply transitively on them.

conclusions: D is a maximal pointed convex cone in V,

There exists an ordered basis $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ of $V$ with $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_i \in \Bbb{R}, c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\},$$

There exists an ordered orthonormal basis $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ of $V$ with $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_i \in \Bbb{R}, c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}.$$
Moreover the map taking $D$ to $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ is a bijection from the maximal pointed convex cones in $V$ to the set of ordered orthonormal bases of $V$.
The orthogonal group $O(V)$ acts simply transitively on the set of maximal pointed convex cones in $V$.

nodes.name: Proof of the classification of maximal pointed convex cones
nodes.statement:
The result is obvious if $n = 1$, since the only maximal pointed convex cones of $\Bbb{R}e_1$ are $\Bbb{R}_{\geq 0}e_1$ and $\Bbb{R}_{\geq 0}(-e_1)$. We use induction on the dimension of $V$. Let $D$ be a maximal pointed convex cone in $V$. From Theorem ef{unique} we know that $D$ has a unique support $H_{v_{n }}$, where $D \subseteq H_{v_{n }}$ and $H_{v_n}^{int} \subseteq D$. From Lemma ef{hyper} we know that we can choose a $v_n$ which is unique with the property that $-v_n \in D$, $||v_n|| = 1$ and $D \subseteq H_{v_{n }}$. Now consider the set $\widetilde{D} = D \cap H(v_{n })$. It is not difficult to see that $\widetilde{D}$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $H(v_{n })$. By induction, we get an orthonormal basis $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n - 1 }\}$ for $H(v_{n })$ such that $$\widetilde{D} = \{x \in H(v_{n }) | <x, v_m> < 0 \ \mbox{for} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | <x, v_m> 
ot= 0\}, 1\leq i \leq n -1 \} \cup \{0\}.$$ Now $D = \{x \in V | <x, v_{n }> < 0\} \cup \widetilde{D}$ and $$D = \{x \in V | <x, v_m> < 0 \ \mbox{for} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | <x, v_m> 
ot= 0\} , 1\leq i \leq n \} \cup \{0\}$$ where $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n\}$ is an orthonormal basis for $V$. This proves that (1) implies (3). That (3) implies (2) is trivial. To show that (2) implies (1), let $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ be an ordered basis of $V$ and let $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}.$$ It is trivial to check that $D$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $V$. Therefore (2) implies (1). Let $D$ be a maximal pointed convex cone in $V$ with $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\} $$ where $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $V$. Suppose $\{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_n\}$ is another orthonormal basis of $V$ for which $$D = \{c_1u_1 + c_2u_2 + \dots + c_nu_n | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}. $$ We have both $H_{u_n}$ and $H_{v_n}$ are supporting half spaces for $D$. Therefore, by Theorem ef{unique} we have $H_{u_n} = H_{v_n}$ and since $||u_n|| = ||v_n|| = 1$, by Lemma ef{hyper}, $u_n = v_n$. Now $ \{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_{n-1} \}$ and $ \{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n-1} \}$ are ordered orthonormal bases of $H = H(u_n) = H(v_n)$ and $\widetilde{D} = D \cap H $ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $H$ with $$\widetilde{D} = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_{n- 1}v_{n-1} | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}$$ $$= \{c_1u_1 + c_2u_2 + \dots + c_{n- 1}u_{n-1} | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}.$$ Hence by induction, we have $ \{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_{n-1} \}$ and $ \{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n-1} \}$ are equal as ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and hence $ \{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_{n-1}, u_n \}$ and\ $ \{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n-1}, v_n \}$ are equal as ordered orthonormal bases of $V$. This shows that the map taking maximal pointed convex cones to ordered orthonormal bases given above is one to one. The map is onto since (3) implies (1). Since the orthogonal group $O(V)$ acts simply transitively on the set of ordered orthonormal bases of $V$, and by linearity the action commutes with the above map from ordered orthonormal bases to maximal pointed convex cones in $V$, we have a simple transitive action of $O(V)$ on the set of maximal pointed convex cones in $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Induct on $\dim V$: peel off the unique support normal $v_n$, apply the inductive hypothesis to $D \cap H(v_n)$, then prove the basis map is bijective and equivariant.

nodes.name: Base case and induction set-up
nodes.statement: The result is obvious if $n = 1$, since the only maximal pointed convex cones of $\Bbb{R}e_1$ are $\Bbb{R}_{\geq 0}e_1$ and $\Bbb{R}_{\geq 0}(-e_1)$. We use induction on the dimension of $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Handle $n=1$ directly and set up induction on $\dim V$.

nodes.name: (1) implies (3) by peeling off the support normal
nodes.statement: Let $D$ be a maximal pointed convex cone in $V$. From Theorem \ref{unique} we know that $D$ has a unique support $H_{v_{n }}$, where $D \subseteq H_{v_{n }}$ and $H_{v_n}^{int} \subseteq D$. From Lemma \ref{hyper} we know that we can choose a $v_n$ which is unique with the property that $-v_n \in D$, $||v_n|| = 1$ and $D \subseteq H_{v_{n }}$. Now consider the set $\widetilde{D} = D \cap H(v_{n })$. It is not difficult to see that $\widetilde{D}$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $H(v_{n })$. By induction, we get an orthonormal basis $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n - 1 }\}$ for $H(v_{n })$ such that $$\widetilde{D} = \{x \in H(v_{n }) | <x, v_m> < 0 \ \mbox{for} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | <x, v_m> \not= 0\}, 1\leq i \leq n -1 \} \cup \{0\}.$$ Now $D = \{x \in V | <x, v_{n }> < 0\} \cup \widetilde{D}$ and $$D = \{x \in V | <x, v_m> < 0 \ \mbox{for} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | <x, v_m> \not= 0\} , 1\leq i \leq n \} \cup \{0\}$$ where $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n\}$ is an orthonormal basis for $V$. This proves that (1) implies (3).
nodes.statement_short: Choose the unique unit $v_n$ with $-v_n \in D$, apply induction to $\widetilde{D} = D\cap H(v_n)$, and reassemble $D$.

nodes.name: (3) implies (2) implies (1)
nodes.statement: That (3) implies (2) is trivial. To show that (2) implies (1), let $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n \}$ be an ordered basis of $V$ and let $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}.$$ It is trivial to check that $D$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $V$. Therefore (2) implies (1).
nodes.statement_short: The first implication is trivial; for the converse check directly that the described $D$ is a maximal pointed convex cone.

nodes.name: The basis map is injective
nodes.statement:
Let $D$ be a maximal pointed convex cone in $V$ with $$D = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_nv_n | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\} $$ where $\{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_n\}$ is an orthonormal basis of $V$. Suppose $\{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_n\}$ is another orthonormal basis of $V$ for which $$D = \{c_1u_1 + c_2u_2 + \dots + c_nu_n | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}. $$ We have both $H_{u_n}$ and $H_{v_n}$ are supporting half spaces for $D$. Therefore, by Theorem ef{unique} we have $H_{u_n} = H_{v_n}$ and since $||u_n|| = ||v_n|| = 1$, by Lemma ef{hyper}, $u_n = v_n$. Now $ \{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_{n-1} \}$ and $ \{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n-1} \}$ are ordered orthonormal bases of $H = H(u_n) = H(v_n)$ and $\widetilde{D} = D \cap H $ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $H$ with $$\widetilde{D} = \{c_1v_1 + c_2v_2 + \dots + c_{n- 1}v_{n-1} | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}$$ $$= \{c_1u_1 + c_2u_2 + \dots + c_{n- 1}u_{n-1} | c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i 
ot= 0 \} \} \cup \{0\}.$$ Hence by induction, we have $ \{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_{n-1} \}$ and $ \{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n-1} \}$ are equal as ordered orthonormal bases of $H$ and hence $ \{u_1, u_2, \dots , u_{n-1}, u_n \}$ and\ $ \{v_1, v_2, \dots , v_{n-1}, v_n \}$ are equal as ordered orthonormal bases of $V$. This shows that the map taking maximal pointed convex cones to ordered orthonormal bases given above is one to one.
nodes.statement_short: Two bases giving the same $D$ share the last vector by the support theorem, then agree by induction inside $H(u_n)$.

nodes.name: The basis map is onto
nodes.statement: The map is onto since (3) implies (1).
nodes.statement_short: Onto follows from (3) implies (1).

nodes.name: Simple transitivity of the $O(V)$-action
nodes.statement: Since the orthogonal group $O(V)$ acts simply transitively on the set of ordered orthonormal bases of $V$, and by linearity the action commutes with the above map from ordered orthonormal bases to maximal pointed convex cones in $V$, we have a simple transitive action of $O(V)$ on the set of maximal pointed convex cones in $V$.
nodes.statement_short: Transport the simply transitive action on ordered orthonormal bases through the bijection.

nodes.name: the poset $\mathcal{L}_n$
nodes.statement: For $n \geq 0$ we let $\mathcal{L}_n$ denote the following poset of subsets of $S^n$ ordered by inclusion: $$\mathcal{L}_n = \{T(\Phi^-_n) \cap \Phi_n^+ | T\in O_{n + 1} \} .$$
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{L}_n$ is the family of sets $T(\Phi_n^-)\cap\Phi_n^+$, $T \in O_{n+1}$, ordered by inclusion.
nodes.genus: poset of subsets of $S^n$ ordered by inclusion

nodes.name: $\Phi_n^+$ is a maximal element of $\mathcal{L}_n$
nodes.statement: Note that $\Phi_n^+ = T(\Phi^-_n)\cap \Phi_n^+$ when $T = -I_{\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}}$. This is a maximal element of $\mathcal{L}_n$.
conclusions: $\Phi_n^+ = T(\Phi^-_n)\cap \Phi_n^+$
This is a maximal element of $\mathcal{L}_n$.

nodes.name: the cone $D_T$ attached to $T \in O_{n+1}$
nodes.statement: If $T \in O_{n + 1}$ with $T(e_i) = v_i$, $1 \leq i \leq n + 1$, we let $$D_T = \{ v = \sum_{i = 1}^{n + 1}c_iv_i \in \Bbb{R}^{n + 1} | <v, v_m> = c_m < 0 \ \mbox{where } \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0\}\} \cup \{0\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: $D_T$ is the cone of vectors whose last nonzero coordinate in the basis $T(e_i)$ is negative.

nodes.name: $D_T$ is a maximal pointed convex cone cutting $S^n$ in $T(\Phi_n^-)$
nodes.statement: It is not difficult to show that $D_T $ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $D_T \cap S^{n} = T(\Phi_n^-)$.
assumptions: $T \in O_{n + 1}$ with $T(e_i) = v_i$, $1 \leq i \leq n + 1$
conclusions: $D_T $ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $D_T \cap S^{n} = T(\Phi_n^-)$

nodes.name: Unique maximal pointed convex cone attached to $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$
nodes.statement: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$, with $X = T_X(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$, then there is a unique maximal pointed convex cone $D_X = D_{T_X}$ in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with the property that $X = D_X \cap \Phi_n^+$.
nodes.statement_short: Every $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$ is cut out of $\Phi_n^+$ by one and only one maximal pointed convex cone $D_X$.
assumptions: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$, with $X = T_X(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$,
conclusions: then there is a unique maximal pointed convex cone $D_X = D_{T_X}$ in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with the property that $X = D_X \cap \Phi_n^+$.

nodes.name: Proof of uniqueness of $D_X$
nodes.statement: From its definition, we have that $D_{T_X}$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $D_{T_X} \cap \Phi_n^+ = T_X(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+ = X$. Suppose that $D$ is another maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $X = D \cap \Phi_n^+$. If $D_e = D_{-I_{\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}}}$, then $\Phi_n^+ = D_e \cap S^n$ and $X = D_X \cap D_e \cap S^n = D \cap D_e \cap S^n$. Now $C_1 = D_X \cap D_e$ and $C_2 = D \cap D_e$ are both convex cones in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $X = C_1 \cap S^n = C_2 \cap S^n$. By Lemma \ref{hatcone}, $\hat{X} = C_1 = C_2$. Let $C'_1 = (D_e \backslash C_1) \cup \{0\} = D_e \cap (-D_X)$. Now $$[C_1 \cup (-C'_1) ] \cup [C'_1 \cup (-C_1)] = D_e \cup (-D_e) = \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$$ and $$[C_1 \cup (-C'_1) ] \cap [C'_1 \cup (-C_1)] = \{0\}$$ since $C_1 \cup (-C'_1) \subseteq D_X$ and $C'_1 \cup (-C_1) \subseteq -D_X$. Since $D_X \cap [C'_1 \cup (-C_1)] = \{0\}$, we can conclude that $D_X = C_1 \cup (-C'_1)$. Since $C'_1 = (D_e \backslash C_2) \cup \{0\} = D_e \cap (-D)$, we can similarly conclude that $D = C_1 \cup (-C'_1)$ and hence $D = D_X$.
nodes.statement_short: Existence is the definition of $D_{T_X}$; uniqueness follows because $\hat{X}$ pins down $D\cap D_e$, and the complementary piece reconstructs $D$.

nodes.name: Existence via $D_{T_X}$
nodes.statement: From its definition, we have that $D_{T_X}$ is a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $D_{T_X} \cap \Phi_n^+ = T_X(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+ = X$.
nodes.statement_short: The cone $D_{T_X}$ already satisfies the requirement.

nodes.name: Reconstructing $D_X$ from $C_1 = D_X \cap D_e$
nodes.statement: Suppose that $D$ is another maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $X = D \cap \Phi_n^+$. If $D_e = D_{-I_{\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}}}$, then $\Phi_n^+ = D_e \cap S^n$ and $X = D_X \cap D_e \cap S^n = D \cap D_e \cap S^n$. Now $C_1 = D_X \cap D_e$ and $C_2 = D \cap D_e$ are both convex cones in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ with $X = C_1 \cap S^n = C_2 \cap S^n$. By Lemma \ref{hatcone}, $\hat{X} = C_1 = C_2$. Let $C'_1 = (D_e \backslash C_1) \cup \{0\} = D_e \cap (-D_X)$. Now $$[C_1 \cup (-C'_1) ] \cup [C'_1 \cup (-C_1)] = D_e \cup (-D_e) = \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$$ and $$[C_1 \cup (-C'_1) ] \cap [C'_1 \cup (-C_1)] = \{0\}$$ since $C_1 \cup (-C'_1) \subseteq D_X$ and $C'_1 \cup (-C_1) \subseteq -D_X$. Since $D_X \cap [C'_1 \cup (-C_1)] = \{0\}$, we can conclude that $D_X = C_1 \cup (-C'_1)$.
nodes.statement_short: Both candidate cones meet $D_e$ in the same cone $\hat{X}$, and $D_X = C_1 \cup (-C_1')$ is forced.

nodes.name: The same reconstruction applies to $D$
nodes.statement: Since $C'_1 = (D_e \backslash C_2) \cup \{0\} = D_e \cap (-D)$, we can similarly conclude that $D = C_1 \cup (-C'_1)$ and hence $D = D_X$.
nodes.statement_short: Repeating the argument for $D$ gives the same formula, so $D = D_X$.

nodes.name: the base cone $D_e$ and the cone $D_X$ of $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$
nodes.statement: We define $D_e = D_{-I_{\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}}}$, that is $$D_e = \{ x = \sum_{i = 1}^{n + 1}c_ie_i \in \Bbb{R}^{n + 1} | <x, e_m> = c_m > 0 \ \mbox{where } \ m = \mbox{max}\{i | c_i \not= 0\}\} \cup \{0\}$$ and $D_e \cap S^n = \Phi_n^+$. For $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$ we let $D_X$ denote the unique maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ for which $X = D_X \cap \Phi_n^+ = D_X \cap D_e \cap S^n$.
nodes.statement_short: $D_e$ is the maximal pointed convex cone with $D_e \cap S^n = \Phi_n^+$, and $D_X$ is the unique cone cutting out $X$.

nodes.name: Alternative characterization of $\mathcal{L}_n$ via maximal pointed convex cones
nodes.statement: Therefore we can characterize $\mathcal{L}_n$ as $$\mathcal{L}_n = \{D\cap \Phi_n^+ | D \ \mbox{is a maximal pointed convex cone in } \ \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: $\mathcal{L}_n$ is exactly the set of intersections of $\Phi_n^+$ with maximal pointed convex cones.
assumptions: D \ \mbox{is a maximal pointed convex cone in } \ \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}
conclusions: $$\mathcal{L}_n = \{D\cap \Phi_n^+ | D \ \mbox{is a maximal pointed convex cone in } \ \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}\}.$$

nodes.name: $\mathcal{L}_0$
nodes.statement: If $n = 0$, then $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1} = \Bbb{R}^1 = \Bbb{R}e_1$. We have $S^0 = \{-e_1, e_1\}, \Phi_0^+ = \{e_1\}$ and $O_1 = \{\pm 1_{e_1}\}$. Therefore $\mathcal{L}_0 = \{\emptyset, \{e_1\}\}$.
nodes.statement_short: For $n = 0$, $\mathcal{L}_0 = \{\emptyset, \{e_1\}\}$.

nodes.name: Self-duality of $\mathcal{L}_n$ via complementation
nodes.statement: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$, then $\Phi^+_n \backslash X$ is also an element of $\mathcal{L}_n$. The map $\phi: \mathcal{L}_n \to \mathcal{L}_n^{\delta}$ given by $\phi(X) = \Phi^+_n \backslash X$ is an order isomorphism of posets.
nodes.statement_short: $X \mapsto \Phi_n^+ \setminus X$ is an order isomorphism $\mathcal{L}_n \to \mathcal{L}_n^{\delta}$.
assumptions: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$,
conclusions: then $\Phi^+_n \backslash X$ is also an element of $\mathcal{L}_n$.
The map $\phi: \mathcal{L}_n \to \mathcal{L}_n^{\delta}$ given by $\phi(X) = \Phi^+_n \backslash X$ is an order isomorphism of posets.

nodes.name: Proof of self-duality of $\mathcal{L}_n$
nodes.statement: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$. There exists a maximal pointed convex cone $D$ in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ for which $X = D \cap \Phi_n^+$. We have that $(-D)$ is also a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ and $(-D)\cap \Phi_n^+ = \Phi_n^+ \backslash X$. Hence $\Phi_n^+ \backslash X \in \mathcal{L}_n$. Since $\phi^2(X) = X$, it is easy to see that $\phi$ is a bijective map. Since $ \Phi_n^+ \backslash X \subseteq \Phi_n^+ \backslash Y$ if and only if $X \supseteq Y$, we have an isomorphism of posets $\phi: \mathcal{L}_n \to \mathcal{L}_n^{\delta}$.
nodes.statement_short: Complementation corresponds to negating the cone $D$, and it is an involution reversing inclusion.

nodes.name: Complement of $X$ lies in $\mathcal{L}_n$
nodes.statement: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$. There exists a maximal pointed convex cone $D$ in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ for which $X = D \cap \Phi_n^+$. We have that $(-D)$ is also a maximal pointed convex cone in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ and $(-D)\cap \Phi_n^+ = \Phi_n^+ \backslash X$. Hence $\Phi_n^+ \backslash X \in \mathcal{L}_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Replace $D$ by $-D$, whose intersection with $\Phi_n^+$ is the complement of $X$.

nodes.name: $\phi$ is an order-reversing bijection
nodes.statement: Since $\phi^2(X) = X$, it is easy to see that $\phi$ is a bijective map. Since $ \Phi_n^+ \backslash X \subseteq \Phi_n^+ \backslash Y$ if and only if $X \supseteq Y$, we have an isomorphism of posets $\phi: \mathcal{L}_n \to \mathcal{L}_n^{\delta}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\phi$ is an involution and reverses inclusion, hence an isomorphism onto the dual poset.

nodes.name: Restriction of $\mathcal{L}_n$ to $\Bbb{R}^n$ lands in $\mathcal{L}_{n-1}$
nodes.statement: Let $X$ be an element of $\mathcal{L}_n$, then $X \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }$ is an element of $\mathcal{L}_{n - 1}$, where $\Bbb{R}^n $ is imbedded in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1} $ as in Section \ref{intro}.
nodes.statement_short: Intersecting an element of $\mathcal{L}_n$ with the imbedded $\Bbb{R}^n$ gives an element of $\mathcal{L}_{n-1}$.
assumptions: Let $X$ be an element of $\mathcal{L}_n$,
where $\Bbb{R}^n $ is imbedded in $\Bbb{R}^{n + 1} $ as in Section \ref{intro}.
conclusions: then $X \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }$ is an element of $\mathcal{L}_{n - 1}$,

nodes.name: Proof that $X \cap \Bbb{R}^n \in \mathcal{L}_{n-1}$
nodes.statement: Given $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$, we have a maximal pointed convex cone $D \subset \Bbb{R}^{n + 1}$ such that $X = D \cap \Phi_n^+$. Let $\widetilde{D} = D \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }$. It is not difficult to see that $\widetilde{D}$ is a maximal pointed convex cone of $\Bbb{R}^{n }$ and therefore $X \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } = D \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+ = \widetilde{D} \cap \Phi_{n - 1}^+ \in \mathcal{L}_{n - 1}$.
nodes.statement_short: Restrict the maximal pointed convex cone $D$ cutting out $X$ to $\Bbb{R}^n$.

nodes.name: Boundary description of $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$
nodes.statement: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$, with $X = T_X(\Phi^-_n)\cap \Phi^+_n$ for some $T_X \in O_{n + 1}$. Let $u_X = T_X(e_{n + 1})$ and $e = -e_{n + 1}$. If $u_X \not= e_{n + 1} = -e$, then \begin{enumerate} \item $X = (X\cap H(u_X)) \cup \{x \in \Phi_n^+ | <x, u_X> < 0 \},$ \item $\bar{X} = [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}] \cap S^n$, \item $\bar{X} \cap S^{n -1} = H_{u_X}\cap S^{n - 1} \supseteq H(u_X)\cap S^{n - 1}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: For $u_X \ne e_{n+1}$, $X$ splits along $H(u_X)$, its closure is $[H_{u_X}\cap H_e]\cap S^n$, and it meets $S^{n-1}$ in $H_{u_X}\cap S^{n-1}$.
assumptions: Let $X \in \mathcal{L}_n$, with $X = T_X(\Phi^-_n)\cap \Phi^+_n$ for some $T_X \in O_{n + 1}$.
Let $u_X = T_X(e_{n + 1})$ and $e = -e_{n + 1}$.
If $u_X \not= e_{n + 1} = -e$,
conclusions: $X = (X\cap H(u_X)) \cup \{x \in \Phi_n^+ | <x, u_X> < 0 \},$
$\bar{X} = [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}] \cap S^n$,
$\bar{X} \cap S^{n -1} = H_{u_X}\cap S^{n - 1} \supseteq H(u_X)\cap S^{n - 1}$.

nodes.name: Proof of the boundary description
nodes.statement: (1) follows from the fact that $X = T_X(\Phi^-_n) \cap \Phi^+_n$ and that $$ T_X(\Phi_n^-) = \{x \in S^n| x = \sum_{i = 1}^{n + 1}c_iT_X(e_i) \ \mbox{such that } \ c_m < 0 , \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i| c_i \not= 0\}\}.$$ Assertion (3) follows from (2) since, given (2), we have $$\bar{X}\cap S^{n -1} = [H_{u_X}\cap S^{n - 1}] \cap [H_{e} \cap S^{n - 1}] \cap [S^n \cap S^{n - 1}] = [H_{u_X}\cap S^{n - 1}] \cap S^{n - 1}.$$ It remains to prove (2). Let $C$ be the convex cone $[H_{u_X}^{int} \cap H_{e}^{int}] \cup \{0\}$, the intersection of the two open half spaces with the zero vector attached. $C$ is non-empty by Lemma \ref{halfspaceintersect}. Now $C \cap S^{n} \subset X \subseteq [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n $ and hence $$ \overline{C \cap S^{n} } \subseteq \overline{X} \subseteq [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n .$$ By Lemma \ref{cone} $$\overline{C} \cap S^{n} \subseteq \overline{X} \subseteq [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n. $$ By Lemma \ref{closure}, $\bar{C} = H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}$. Therefore $\overline{X} = [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n$ and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Assertions (1) and (3) are immediate from the definitions and (2); (2) itself follows by taking closures of $H_{u_X}^{int}\cap H_e^{int}$.

nodes.name: Assertion (1) from the description of $T_X(\Phi_n^-)$
nodes.statement: (1) follows from the fact that $X = T_X(\Phi^-_n) \cap \Phi^+_n$ and that $$ T_X(\Phi_n^-) = \{x \in S^n| x = \sum_{i = 1}^{n + 1}c_iT_X(e_i) \ \mbox{such that } \ c_m < 0 , \ \mbox{where} \ m = \mbox{max}\{i| c_i \not= 0\}\}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Expand $T_X(\Phi_n^-)$ in the basis $T_X(e_i)$.

nodes.name: Assertion (3) deduced from (2)
nodes.statement: Assertion (3) follows from (2) since, given (2), we have $$\bar{X}\cap S^{n -1} = [H_{u_X}\cap S^{n - 1}] \cap [H_{e} \cap S^{n - 1}] \cap [S^n \cap S^{n - 1}] = [H_{u_X}\cap S^{n - 1}] \cap S^{n - 1}.$$
nodes.statement_short: Intersect the formula of (2) with $S^{n-1}$.

nodes.name: Set-up for (2): the cone $C$ of the two open half spaces
nodes.statement: It remains to prove (2). Let $C$ be the convex cone $[H_{u_X}^{int} \cap H_{e}^{int}] \cup \{0\}$, the intersection of the two open half spaces with the zero vector attached. $C$ is non-empty by Lemma \ref{halfspaceintersect}.
nodes.statement_short: Introduce $C = [H_{u_X}^{int}\cap H_e^{int}]\cup\{0\}$, non-empty by the half-space intersection lemma.

nodes.name: Squeeze $\bar{X}$ between the two closures
nodes.statement: Now $C \cap S^{n} \subset X \subseteq [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n $ and hence $$ \overline{C \cap S^{n} } \subseteq \overline{X} \subseteq [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n .$$ By Lemma \ref{cone} $$\overline{C} \cap S^{n} \subseteq \overline{X} \subseteq [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n. $$ By Lemma \ref{closure}, $\bar{C} = H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}$. Therefore $\overline{X} = [H_{u_X} \cap H_{e}]\cap S^n$ and the result follows.
nodes.statement_short: Sandwich $\overline{X}$ using $\overline{C\cap S^n} = \bar{C}\cap S^n$ and $\bar{C} = H_{u_X}\cap H_e$.

nodes.name: Equality of the traces of the hyperplanes $H(u_X), H(u_Y)$ on $\Bbb{R}^n$
nodes.statement: Let $X$, $Y \in \mathcal{L}_n$ with $X = T_X(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$ and $Y = T_Y(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$. Let $u_X = T_X(e_{n + 1})$ and let $u_Y = T_Y(e_{n + 1})$. If $H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } \not= \Bbb{R}^{n }$ and $H(u_X) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } \subseteq H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }$, then $$H(u_X) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } = H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }.$$
nodes.statement_short: If $H(u_Y)$ cuts $\Bbb{R}^n$ properly and $H(u_X)\cap\Bbb{R}^n$ is contained in it, the two traces coincide.
assumptions: Let $X$, $Y \in \mathcal{L}_n$ with $X = T_X(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$ and $Y = T_Y(\Phi_n^-) \cap \Phi_n^+$. Let $u_X = T_X(e_{n + 1})$ and let $u_Y = T_Y(e_{n + 1})$.
If $H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } \not= \Bbb{R}^{n }$ and $H(u_X) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } \subseteq H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }$, then
conclusions: $$H(u_X) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } = H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n }.$$

nodes.name: Proof by dimension count
nodes.statement: We have $ H(u_Y)\cap \Bbb{R}^{n } $ is a subspace of $\Bbb{R}^{n}$ of dimension $n$ or of dimension $n - 1$ . Since we are assuming that $H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^{n } \not= \Bbb{R}^{n }$, it must be a subspace of dimension $n - 1$. Since $H(u_X) \cap \Bbb{R}^n \subseteq H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^n$ it too must be a subspace of dimension $n - 1$ and hence must be all of $H(u_Y) \cap \Bbb{R}^n$.
nodes.statement_short: Both traces are $(n-1)$-dimensional subspaces of $\Bbb{R}^n$, so containment forces equality.

nodes.name: Splitting of $T_Z$ when $H(u_Z) = \Bbb{R}^n$
nodes.statement: Let $Z \in \mathcal{L}_n$, with $Z = T_Z(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+$ for some $T_Z \in O_{n + 1}$. Let $u_Z = T_Z(e_{n + 1})$. If $H(u_Z) = \Bbb{R}^n$, then $T_Z = T'_Z \bot \pm 1_{e_{n + 1}}$ for some $T'_Z \in O_n$.
nodes.statement_short: If $T_Z$ preserves $\Bbb{R}^n$ then it splits as $T'_Z \bot \pm 1_{e_{n+1}}$ with $T'_Z \in O_n$.
assumptions: Let $Z \in \mathcal{L}_n$, with $Z = T_Z(\Phi_n^-)\cap \Phi_n^+$ for some $T_Z \in O_{n + 1}$.
Let $u_Z = T_Z(e_{n + 1})$. If $H(u_Z) = \Bbb{R}^n$, then
conclusions: $T_Z = T'_Z \bot \pm 1_{e_{n + 1}}$ for some $T'_Z \in O_n$.

nodes.name: Proof of the splitting of $T_Z$
nodes.statement: Since $T_Z$ is an isometry, with $T_Z(\Bbb{R}^n) = H(u_Z) = \Bbb{R}^n$, we have $T_Z|_{\Bbb{R}^n} = T'_Z \in O_n$. Now $||u_Z|| = 1$ and $<u_Z, x> = 0$ for all $x \in \Bbb{R}^n$. Hence $u_Z = \pm e_{n + 1}$ and $T_Z = T'_Z\bot \pm 1_{e_{n + 1}}$.
nodes.statement_short: $T_Z$ restricts to an isometry of $\Bbb{R}^n$ and $u_Z$ must be $\pm e_{n+1}$.

nodes.name: Joins exist in $\mathcal{L}_0$ (induction base)
nodes.statement: We will use induction to find $X \vee Y$ for two elements $X$ and $Y$ of $\mathcal{L}_n$. Obviously we can find $X\vee Y$ in $\mathcal{L}_0$ for any pair of elements $\{X, Y\}$ in $\mathcal{L}_0$.
nodes.section: 5 The least upper bound of two elements of $\mathcal{L}_n$
nodes.statement_short: Any two elements of $\mathcal{L}_0$ have a join, giving the base of the induction on $n$.
assumptions: for two elements $X$ and $Y$ of $\mathcal{L}_n$
conclusions: Obviously we can find $X\vee Y$ in $\mathcal{L}_0$ for any pair of elements $\{X, Y\}$ in $\mathcal{L}_0$.
